summary.text: 南 is attested for “south” in Shang inscriptions. Its early graph is commonly understood as a picture of an object, though the proposed object—such as a musical instrument, a house front, or a covered vessel—is disputed.

formation.text: The early graph is pictographic, but its depicted object is uncertain. Proposals include a hanging percussion instrument, a house front, and a covered vessel with a plant-like feature above; the vessel account links it to 醓, “meat sauce.” The received Shuowen analysis divides the graph into 𣎵 and 𢆉 and assigns 𢆉 a phonetic role, but the available evidence does not independently verify that sound relation.

history.text: 南 is recorded in oracle-bone, bronze, manuscript, and seal forms. The ancient form 𡴖 is also recorded, but the available accounts do not establish a continuous graphic sequence from Shang forms to the later character.

Shang inscriptions use 南 for the direction, in the ancestor name 南庚, and for a sacrificial item. Under one borrowing proposal, an early graph for an object was reused to write “south” because the object-name and “south” sounded alike or similar. The object’s identity and ancient name and pronunciation remain unresolved, and the inscriptions do not establish which use came first.

uncertainties.text: The early graph’s referent remains disputed among instrument, house-front, covered-vessel, and other proposals. A proposed lexical link between “south” and a belly or front-of-body word concerns the spoken word’s history; it does not establish the graph’s formation or a semantic path.
The exact earliest inscription and the order of the reported Shang uses are unresolved; a continuous graphic derivation is also not established.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone inscriptions; exact earliest specimen date unresolved
senses.text: 南 is attested for the direction “south” in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions. This establishes an early use, not that “south” was the graph’s original meaning.
南 is also used for a southern part; its date relative to the directional sense is unresolved.
南 is also used to mean southward; its date relative to the directional sense is unresolved.

limitations.text: The reported ancestor-name and sacrificial-item uses do not establish separate character senses or a chronology among the Shang uses.

Instrument-name borrowing is a reported proposal, not a verified explanation: the proposed instrument’s identity, ancient name, and pronunciation are unresolved, and the reported Shang uses do not establish that the directional word was borrowed from its name.
The proposed lexical link between “south” and a belly or front-of-body word does not establish a semantic development.

overview.text: 南 means “south,” a use attested in Shang inscriptions. One proposal is that an early object sign was reused to write “south” because the words sounded alike or similar; the object, its name, and the sound match remain unresolved.
